title: Pricing by hours per project for Real estate portfolio management
audience: Owners and supervisors of small portfolio management businesses who price management work and project work, such as a vacancy re-let or a property condition report, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the business's own figures
Estimate hours for property tasks, including inspections, tenant work, maintenance coordination, records and checking time
Build a fee or a project quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: Portfolio work is made of many small tasks: listing a vacancy, showing the property, checking references, preparing the lease, inspecting at each change of tenant, chasing a late payment, booking a tradesperson, and reporting to the owner. Each one takes time, and the time differs from property to property. Once the hours are known, the cost, the margin and the effect of a change in scope can be seen. A fee with no hours behind it hides risk and waste, and it cannot be defended when an owner asks why the fee is what it is. No source in the research gives typical management hours per property, or a fee benchmark, so the hours must come from the business's own records.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in that period. Total cost includes wages with on-costs, such as leave and superannuation, where your staff arrangements require them, vehicle running costs, property management software, trust account administration, insurance, professional fees, equipment, administration and premises. Productive hours are the hours spent on chargeable work for owners, not the paid hours on a roster. Business.gov.au lists on-costs such as leave and superannuation as part of the hourly cost (Choose a pricing strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026). If a manager is paid for 40 hours and 30 are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage. Use the business's own figures, dated, and not a figure from another manager.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break the portfolio work into tasks for each property: the monthly routine, inspections, each tenancy event, and each maintenance job. Estimate each at a standard speed for your own team, then add travel between properties, set-up, reporting, and a checking allowance. Use ranges where the work is uncertain. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as tenant absence at an inspection or a tradesperson who does not attend. One guide suggests adding 10 to 20 percent to job estimates for unexpected work (Xero Australia, How to price services, 3 September 2026). That is a general service-business range, not a property management figure, so check it against your own records. After each month, record the actual hours for each property and the reason for any gap.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the work. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk, such as a difficult owner, a property in poor condition, or a complex tenancy. One author presents a gross margin of at least 20 percent as a floor, and says the right figure varies by business and market (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025). That is one author's view. Apply the trust account rules for money you hold, and your minimum charge. Where the fee is a monthly amount, convert the hours into a monthly figure for each property and check that the fee covers it. Where the work is a project, such as a vacancy re-let, price it as a separate quote with its own scope.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A management quote or appointment should state the scope, the fee basis, the exclusions, what the owner must provide or approve, and how long the terms apply. Exclusions usually include major works, legal action and tax advice. Do not show the internal cost per hour unless your policy says to. Record every change to the scope, and re-quote when it changes. Queensland law says commission must be disclosed in the appointment and may be claimed only for actual amounts (Property Occupations Act 2014, sections 105 and 88; excerpt read only). NSW guidance says a written agency agreement is needed for payment of commissions and costs, for short-term rental (NSW Fair Trading, Property management, published 19 June 2025, modified 6 October 2026).

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare the estimated and actual hours for each property type for at least the first ten properties or the first three months of a new portfolio. If the gap is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is not finished when it is written. It is finished when actual hours match the fee basis closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break the portfolio work into property tasks and estimate each task time as a range.
Add travel, set-up, reporting and checking time as named lines.
Multiply total hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin for risk and target.
Apply the trust account rules and the minimum charge.
Write the appointment or quote with scope, fee basis, exclusions, owner inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each month and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not market rates or fee benchmarks. A manager looks after three units. The monthly routine for each unit is estimated at 1.5 hours, and the manager's cost per productive hour is $75 (hypothetical). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (hypothetical).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the monthly cost of the routine work for the three units, what is the price at a 25 per cent margin on price, and what changes if one unit has a tenancy change that takes 4 extra hours?
workedExamples.reasoning: The routine cost is 3 units multiplied by 1.5 hours, which is 4.5 hours, at $75 an hour, which is $337.50 a month. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $450 a month. A tenancy change adds 4 hours, or $300 at $75 an hour. That extra work is charged only if the appointment allows it, and then the cost becomes $637.50 and the price becomes $850, with the extra quote shown separately. The manager does not take these figures as a fee for other portfolios, because the research found no fee benchmark.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote or fee worksheet, with property-by-property hours
Time log for each property, with estimated and actual columns
Property condition report template with photos
PPE as listed in {{business:safety.required_ppe}} for any site visit

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, software, trust administration, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel between properties, reporting and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.

commonErrors.error: Setting a fee with no exclusions or no fee basis in writing
commonErrors.prevention: List what is excluded, the fee basis, and what the owner must approve or provide.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each month and review the variance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026). State rules on agency fees, commissions and trust money also apply and differ between states.

Money held for owners must follow the trust rules for the state. In NSW, deposits are trust money paid into the agent's trust account, but the NSW page read covers short-term rental only, so long-term rules are not confirmed. In Victoria, owners corporation managers must hold money in trust and avoid mixing it, but that applies to strata management, not residential rental management. Confirm the rule for each state where you hold money.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates. Letting and rent collection for reward can need a licence, so check the licence rule in each state before taking on the work.

qualityStandard: Each appointment or quote shows scope, fee or price basis, exclusions, owner inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the business's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for each property type for at least the first ten properties or three months, and compared with the estimate.
No appointment is issued without a margin decision, a trust-money check and a licence check for the work in the state.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Appointment or quote showing scope, fee basis, exclusions and validity
Property time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make portfolio work visible, so start every appointment from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Travel, reporting and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid staff member, and nothing else from the accounts
The fee the owner pays, plus any deposit and late fee
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, software, trust administration, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours
The average fee charged by competitors, taken from their websites

knowledgeChecks.question: A property routine is estimated at 5 hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Leave the estimate, since the owner has already paid for the month
Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future appointments
Reduce paid hours for staff on the next property and skip the reporting
Raise the fee for this owner only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does an appointment need an exclusions list and a fee basis?
options: To hide the margin from the owner and keep the rates secret from staff
To show what the fee covers, so extra work can be priced and disputes are reduced
To make the appointment longer and fill the page with more text
To lower the owner's expectations and make the work seem smaller than it is

sourceReferences: ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as leave and superannuation belong in the hourly cost.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; a 10 to 20 per cent buffer for unexpected work (general service range, not a property management figure).

Carters Trade Leader, 'Estimating how many hours a job will take', https://tradeleader.carters.co.nz/trade-skills/estimating-how-many-hours-a-job-will-take-why-83-get-it-wrong/, dated 1 October 2025. New Zealand publisher. Supports: comparing quoted and actual labour to correct the next quote. The 20 per cent gross margin floor is one author's view.

Markel Direct, 'How to price a job as a tradesperson', https://www.markeluk.com/knowledge-centre/how-to-price-a-job-as-a-tradesperson, dated 12 August 2026. Supports: listing every task before estimating hours.

Queensland legislation, Property Occupations Act 2014, https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/pdf/current/act-2014-022, current as at 6 June 2025. Excerpt only. Supports: commission may be claimed only for actual amounts (section 88); commission must be disclosed in the appointment (section 105).

NSW Fair Trading, 'Property management', https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/property-management, published 19 June 2025, modified 6 October 2026. Covers short-term rental only. Supports: a written agency agreement is needed for commissions and costs.

consumer.vic.gov.au, 'Owners corporation managers: financial information', https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/licensing-and-registration/owners-corporation-managers/running-your-business/financial-information, last updated 30 November 2017. Applies to strata management only.
